The new beryllium plasma facing surface represents ~40 m2 of the ~80 m2 replaced by the ITER-like wall.
The beryllium tiles have an electrical resistivity of ~0.08 μΩm at 200°C, much lower than the previous carbon tiles.
The design limit for the exposed depth of the beryllium tiles was ~40 μm, combined with a minimum cut width of 350 μm.
The optimum castellation size for the beryllium tiles was 12 mm × 12 mm with a half-round profile.
JET had ~4,000 kg of beryllium available for re-use, which helped achieve the target iron concentration of 0.075%.
Two EDM rates were tested, with the faster rate of 3.03 cc/hr selected for the castellation machining.
The flash etch process using a 1% HF-25% HNO3 solution was found to provide the best chemical and geometrical properties for the castellations.
A total of 227 anomalies were recorded during the installation of the beryllium PFCs, with 159 resulting in non-conformance reports and modifications.
Disruptions caused the melting of the outermost upper dump plate tiles due to field line penetration through large gaps.
Slide-away electron beams caused localized damage on the inner wall guard limiter, but the overall damage was found to have only a marginal increase over the operating period.
The main chamber power handling achieved and possibly exceeded the design targets, with the measured and computed power footprints being very similar.
Restarting the plasma on the ITER-like wall proved much easier than for the carbon wall, with no further conditioning required after the first plasma.
The higher elongation limiter configuration was run with up to 5 MW additional heating and 1 MW ohmic heating for over 7 seconds on the inner wall.
The monitored temperature on the inner wall stayed below 760°C, but some beams outside the monitored regions reached far higher temperatures with apparent melting damage.
The design of the beryllium PFCs was the result of a complex compromise to satisfy requirements and technical boundary conditions.
